title: GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Opus 5.5 vs Gemini: Which Is Worth Paying For? API Pricing, Worked Out
description:
Three jobs people actually run every month, priced on GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Grok 4.7 and Gemini 3.8 Flash with the official list prices of September 28, 2026. The winner is not the smartest model, and the video ends with the three-question test that turns this math into yours.

Every price comes from the vendor's own pricing page on the recording date and will change; the formula is on screen so you can redo it with today's numbers. The picks at the end are the channel host's personal opinion, and the video labels them as such. No model was benchmarked here; the only measurement is arithmetic on published prices.

Recorded 2026-09-28.

chapters.hook: Three price sheets, one month of work
chapters.sheet: Official API prices for five models, side by side
chapters.formula: How token costs add up: the formula and job one
chapters.job2: Job two: a coding agent for a month
chapters.job3: Job three: a support bot, 10,000 chats a month
chapters.retry: When the expensive model is cheaper
chapters.test: The three-question test, and my picks
chapters.outro: So which one is worth paying for?

iut8.text: GPT-6 Astra costs fifty dollars per million output tokens. Claude Opus 5.5 costs twenty. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs under four.

4f5z.text: Pick by benchmark and you overpay. Pick by price and you get work you have to redo.

ed4s.text: So I priced three jobs people actually run every month, on every model, at today's official rates.

4vsv.text: The winner isn't the smartest model. Here's the math, and the three questions that make it your math.

zeh4.text: First, the price sheets side by side, read from each company's own pricing page today.

mpni.text: OpenAI's flagship, GPT-6 Astra: ten dollars in, one dollar for cached input, fifty out, per million tokens.

bgt8.text: OpenAI's cheaper sibling, GPT-6 Sol: two in, twenty cents cached, ten out.

a8eb.text: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5: four in, twenty cents cached, twenty out.

xiua.text: xAI's Grok 4.7, for prompts under two hundred thousand tokens: two in, fifty cents cached, six out.

qx54.text: Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash: seventy-five cents in, seven and a half cents cached, three dollars seventy-five out.

39yb.text: Google says that Flash price holds until the end of the year and then doubles. It lists no Pro price for the 3.8 generation yet.

493h.text: The formula fits on one slide. Tokens in times the input price, cached tokens times the cached price, plus tokens out times the output price.

yvm3.text: Job one: summarize a forty-page PDF every morning. Thirty thousand tokens in, a thousand out, thirty days a month.

uia6.text: That's under a million tokens in, and thirty thousand out. Watch how little that costs anywhere.

uwys.text: Astra, ten dollars fifty a month. Opus 5.5, four dollars twenty.

d8vw.text: Sol, two dollars ten. Gemini Flash, seventy-nine cents. Grok sits at about two dollars.

gjky.text: For a job like this the gap is real, but it's pocket money. The question is quality, and any of these can summarize a PDF.

afk4.text: Job two is where the money goes: a coding agent working beside you all day, twenty workdays a month.

xupq.text: Every turn it re-reads the whole conversation, so most of its input is cached. Say six hundred thousand fresh tokens a day.

ph5f.text: Plus two point four million cached and a hundred fifty thousand out, daily.

xexs.text: Twenty workdays: twelve million fresh, forty-eight million cached, three million out. Now the prices bite.

wz7s.text: Astra: about three hundred forty-eight dollars a month. A hundred fifty of that is cache writes, a fee OpenAI lists for its newer models.

mcai.text: Sol, the cheaper OpenAI model: about seventy. Opus 5.5: about one hundred thirty, sixty of it cache writes.

z6g3.text: Grok 4.7: about sixty-six. Gemini 3.8 Flash: about twenty-four.

tnfs.text: Neither lists a cache write fee, though Google bills hourly cache storage, which I left out.

cv6f.text: Same work, almost a fifteen-fold price range. This is the job where picking wrong costs you hundreds a month, or a lot of rework.

zyt2.text: Job three: a support bot. Ten thousand chats a month, three thousand tokens in and three hundred out each. Thirty million in, three million out.

4e86.text: Astra: four hundred fifty. Opus 5.5: one eighty.

gbsu.text: Grok 4.7: seventy-eight. Gemini Flash: thirty-four. Sol lands at ninety.

b3ge.text: Notice where the money goes: input. A support bot reads far more than it writes, so the input price matters most.

dsie.text: Now the twist. The bill isn't just the API. If the cheap model needs you to fix its work, your time goes on the bill.

mbxu.text: Take the coding job on Gemini Flash at twenty-four dollars, and suppose it costs you one hour a week of fixing.

pmjw.text: At forty dollars an hour, that's about one hundred sixty dollars more, roughly one eighty-four in total.

xauy.text: Opus 5.5 at one hundred thirty, with fewer retries, is now the cheaper option. Change the hour or the rate and it flips back.

bxqs.text: Those two numbers, the hour and the rate, are mine, as an example. Yours are the ones that count, and only you can measure them.

pdgg.text: The rule behind the twist: retries multiply everything. Two tries at a low price can cost more than one at a high price.

h2z3.text: So the real question is never which model is smartest. It's which model's failure rate you can afford on your job, at the lowest price.

trey.text: Here's the test I use before paying for any model. Three questions.

f4vb.text: One, what does a wrong answer cost? If it's cheap to check, buy cheap. If it's expensive to undo, pay up.

tqzv.text: Two, how many retries do I really do? Count them for a week. Most people guess low.

ez5e.text: Three, is the cheaper sibling good enough? Every lab sells one: Sol under Astra, Flash under Pro, the smaller Claude models under Opus.

wpuc.text: My picks, and these are opinions, not measurements. For the daily summary, the cheapest model that reads well; the money is trivial.

m4uq.text: For the coding agent, I'd start with Opus 5.5 or Sol, count retries for a week, then decide.

6cnv.text: For the support bot, I'd pick Flash or Grok with a checking step, because input volume drives that bill.

msvn.text: And I wouldn't switch because a new model topped a chart this week. I switch when my cost, quality or speed actually changes.

d539.text: By the way, the agent from the last video fetched two of these price pages for us, and hit a wall on the third.

a6h2.text: That run, wall included, is in the previous video.

u2g7.text: So which one is worth paying for? The one whose mistakes on your job you can afford, at the lowest price that gets you there.

y5p9.text: Price your own month with the formula, count your retries for a week, and add the cost of being wrong. Then decide.

ypij.text: Every price in this video is from the vendors' own pages on September 28, 2026, and they will change. The links are in the description.
